Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
Traffic flows past construction work on eastbound Highway 50 in Sacramento on Aug. 12, 2021. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build environmentally ruinous projects.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 17, 2026
What’s the most polarizing four-letter word in California politics?
CEQA.
That wasn’t always the case. When then-Gov. Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act into law in 1970, the need could not have been more obvious. Californians were fed up with planners bulldozing low-income neighborhoods and communities of color for miles of polluting freeways. They were horrified by the ecological damage and habitat destruction caused by suburban sprawl. They were tired of top-down infrastructure projects that left communities feeling disempowered and voiceless.
CEQA laid out a basic protective framework: Before approving a project, government officials needed to evaluate potential negative environmental impacts and identify ways to mitigate or avoid them while providing ample opportunity for public review and input.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But it didn’t take long for the law to be easily manipulated for ends that had little or nothing to do with the environment.
NIMBYs used the process to delay new infill housing — driving up costs and reducing the likelihood projects get built. Unions leveraged CEQA to extort favorable labor terms on projects (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-housing-union-labor-17802611.php). Courts showed a predisposition for allowing just about anything to become grounds for a CEQA challenge — which is how we ended up with a 2022 lawsuit against a UC Berkeley housing project (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-UC-Berkeley-students-are-now-16931016.php) that effectively branded students as a form of pollution.
This editorial board has repeatedly decried CEQA abuses and has urged politicians to take decisive action (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/uc-berkeley-peoples-park-housing-ceqa-newsom-17816129.php).
In recent years, they have, to a degree.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
State lawmakers passed, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, bills to, among other things, permit more units on many single-family-home lots (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/California-cities-rush-to-limit-new-law-16647764.php), streamline the development of dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/sb79-now-law-fight-affordable-housing-goes-21094908.php), exempt almost all infill housing from CEQA (https://sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) and speed up permitting timelines for large clean-energy projects (https://modelclimatelaws.org/resources/californias-sb-205-2022/).
But it’s still far too easy to bury certain essential projects in delay, litigation and costly uncertainty.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.

Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.

PROPOSITION 45
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section
21010) is added to Division 13 of the Public Resources
Code, to read:
CHAPTER 1.5. BUILDING AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA ACT
Article 1. Title, Findings and Declarations,
and Purpose
21010. Title
This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Building an Affordable California Act.
21011. Findings and Declarations
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare all of the following:
(a) California’s outdated system for approving essential
projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly.
Essential projects like clean water, clean energy,
hospitals, affordable housing, roads, wildfire
prevention, schools, public safety, and other
infrastructure improvements are being delayed or
blocked by unnecessary red tape, bureaucratic delays,
and excessive lawsuits.
(b) These delays substantially increase the cost of
living for all Californians. Research shows that
permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars
to the price of a new home, driving up rents and
mortgages for homeowners and renters. Similar red
tape adds billions of dollars to the cost of building
hospitals, water infrastructure, roads, bridges, clean
energy, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation
projects, costs ultimately passed on to consumers and
taxpayers.
(c) California’s permitting laws were written more than
50 years ago, before today’s modern environmental
laws were in place. That outdated system now works
against the state’s environmental and public health
goals by slowing down or blocking essential projects
that would reduce air pollution, lower greenhouse gas
emissions, safeguard water supplies, protect
communities from wildfire, and preserve wildlife and
the environment.
(d) The act will modernize and streamline state law to
cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays, limit
frivolous lawsuits that block essential projects while
allowing public agencies and essential project
applicants to continue sharing the burden of defending
against those suits, and speed up delivery of projects
Californians rely on every day.
(e) Every year of delay means Californians wait longer
and pay more for the things they need most. The act
applies to the state’s most essential projects, including:
(1) Clean drinking water and secure water supplies for
communities across the state.
(2) Safe, modern hospitals and clinics to ensure access
to affordable health care.
(3) Clean energy and reliable electricity to reduce
energy bills and fight climate change.
(4) Housing of all types in order to make housing more
affordable for families struggling with skyrocketing
rents and mortgages as well as vulnerable senior
populations.
(5) Roads, bridges, and transit to cut traffic congestion
and improve public safety.
(6) Wildfire prevention and resilience projects to
protect lives, homes, and natural resources.
(7) Safe, modernized public schools and educational
facilities for students and educators.
(8) Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
to connect underserved communities and expand
opportunity.
(f) By speeding up these essential projects, the act will
make California more affordable and lower the cost of
housing, energy, electricity, health care, and other
necessities, while also reducing taxpayer costs for
public works projects.
(g) The act will also jump-start projects that create
well-paying jobs and put tens of thousands of
Californians to work, especially in construction, clean
energy, and infrastructure, helping grow California’s
economy when it is needed most.
(h) Importantly, the act maintains state and federal
clean air, clean water, and environmental protection
laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the Safe
Drinking Water Act, the federal Toxic Substances
Control Act, the federal Clean Water Act, the Clean Air
Act, the federal Environmental Quality Improvement
Act, the California Global Warming Solutions Act, the
California Coastal Act, and the federal Resource
Conservation and Recovery Act. This chapter will help
build the projects needed to make California more
affordable, without repealing these laws that keep
families and the environment safe.
(i) We can and must build an affordable California.
21012. Statement of Purpose

(a) In order to maximize the ability to streamline and

Chris Elmendorf (UC Davis, pro-housing law prof): mixed, uncertain. Deborah Sivas (Stanford Law): "meat axe," judicial review constraints make CEQA "meaningless." Darrell Steinberg (former Senate leader, Sacramento mayor, CEQA reform supporter): opposes — initiative should be last resort; legislature is actively reforming.

- YIMBY split: YIMBY Action neutral; Housing Action Coalition and CA Council for Affordable Housing support; some affordable housing groups oppose. NYT: Tejon Ranch (sprawl developer) backing; "embraces sprawl."

- Rural County Representatives of California: neutral (policy advocate wanted to oppose—goes too far, puts power in developers' hands, limits local authority).

- League of California Cities / CSAC: mostly stayed out/neutral.

- Gov. Newsom: no position. Republican Party: yes. CA Democratic Party: no.

- Data centers: disputed whether covered; likely litigation.

- Exclusions: Delta tunnel, nuclear, high-speed rail, jails (poll-tested exclusions).

- Tribal consultation limited to federally recognized tribes — LA Times: dozens of non-recognized tribes sidelined; major Yes contributor is Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation (federally recognized tribe).

- Judicial review: courts can only halt portions with "specific, adverse impact upon public safety"; 270-day limit incl. appeals (+90 extension); record limited to timely comments; "fullest possible weight" interpretive clause toward approval.

- AIA|LA individual author: "Yes, with two reservations... more discomfort than anything else on this ballot." Interesting nuanced yes.

Arguments for Yes:
- CEQA is genuinely abused (NIMBY lawsuits against infill housing, bike lanes, transit; UC Berkeley case; union "greenmail"). Broad consensus across the spectrum that CEQA needs reform. Even SF Chronicle (No) agrees deadlines/paperwork reduction are reasonable.
- Deadlines (365 days EIR, 270 days courts) address real dysfunction — e.g., Richardson Grove 15 years of litigation.
- Housing crisis is California's biggest problem; permitting delays add cost ($75k/home per CBIA, though self-interested).
- Clean energy and transit projects need faster buildout for climate goals — there's an "abundance" argument that CEQA now impedes environmental goals (transmission, etc.).
- Support from affordable housing groups, children's hospitals, water association, clean energy groups (American Clean Power), NAACP/LULAC, Environmental Policy Innovation Center (a centrist enviro group).
- 26 newspaper endorsements including McClatchy CA papers, Mercury News/East Bay Times, SDUT, WSJ.

Arguments for No:
- Goes far beyond streamlining: shifts power to applicants (one alternative instead of range; standards frozen at application; agencies can't request more info; comment caps; record limits; courts can't halt projects except portions with "specific adverse impact upon public safety"; interpretive clause favoring approval).
- Blanket approach covers freeway expansions, greenfield sprawl in fire zones, warehouses, possibly data centers — not just infill housing/clean energy. Poll-tested exclusions (HSR, Delta tunnel, nuclear) undermine the "good policy" rationale.
- 2025 reforms (AB 130/SB 131) already exempted most infill housing — so marginal housing benefit mostly accrues to sprawl.
- Legislature is actively reforming CEQA; initiative locks in a 41-page statutory regime that is hard to fix (needs further ballot measures for major changes — need to verify amendment provision; the AIA piece mentioned Section 21032 severability; let me check amendment section in text).
- Non-federally recognized tribes lose consultation rights.
- Funded by utilities (Edison, Sempra), developers (CBIA, Tejon Ranch), Chamber — interests that profit; no affordability requirements in the measure.
- Opposition from essentially every environmental/public health group, nurses, plus State Building Trades, SEIU, CA Democratic Party; Stanford/Berkeley law experts critical.
- LAO: upfront costs high tens of millions to >$100M/yr; uncertain net.
- Judicial review constraints could make CEQA effectively unenforceable for covered projects (Sivas).
- Polling trending No; Newsom neutral; many CEQA reformers oppose as overreach.

The balance: This is a close call politically, but the weight of expert opinion (CEQA-reform-friendly voices like Steinberg, Elmendorf's caution, Elkind's "sea change," the YIMBY split, Rural Counties' discomfort, SF Chronicle's "even messier") suggests the measure overreaches: it bundles reasonable deadline reforms with deep structural changes to judicial review and alternatives analysis, applies them to a poll-tested grab bag including freeways and sprawl, ambiguously data centers, and locks them in via initiative statute.

PROPOSITION 45
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds sections to the Public
Resources Code; therefore, new provisions proposed to
be added are printed in italic type to indicate that they
are new.
PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section
21010) is added to Division 13 of the Public Resources
Code, to read:
CHAPTER 1.5. BUILDING AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA ACT
Article 1. Title, Findings and Declarations,
and Purpose
21010. Title
This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Building an Affordable California Act.
21011. Findings and Declarations
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare all of the following:
(a) California’s outdated system for approving essential
projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly.
Essential projects like clean water, clean energy,
hospitals, affordable housing, roads, wildfire
prevention, schools, public safety, and other
infrastructure improvements are being delayed or
blocked by unnecessary red tape, bureaucratic delays,
and excessive lawsuits.
(b) These delays substantially increase the cost of
living for all Californians. Research shows that
permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars
to the price of a new home, driving up rents and
mortgages for homeowners and renters. Similar red
tape adds billions of dollars to the cost of building
hospitals, water infrastructure, roads, bridges, clean
energy, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation
projects, costs ultimately passed on to consumers and
taxpayers.
(c) California’s permitting laws were written more than
50 years ago, before today’s modern environmental
laws were in place. That outdated system now works
against the state’s environmental and public health
goals by slowing down or blocking essential projects
that would reduce air pollution, lower greenhouse gas
emissions, safeguard water supplies, protect
communities from wildfire, and preserve wildlife and
the environment.
(d) The act will modernize and streamline state law to
cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays, limit
frivolous lawsuits that block essential projects while
allowing public agencies and essential project
applicants to continue sharing the burden of defending
against those suits, and speed up delivery of projects
Californians rely on every day.
(e) Every year of delay means Californians wait longer
and pay more for the things they need most. The act
applies to the state’s most essential projects, including:
(1) Clean drinking water and secure water supplies for
communities across the state.
(2) Safe, modern hospitals and clinics to ensure access
to affordable health care.
(3) Clean energy and reliable electricity to reduce
energy bills and fight climate change.
(4) Housing of all types in order to make housing more
affordable for families struggling with skyrocketing
rents and mortgages as well as vulnerable senior
populations.
(5) Roads, bridges, and transit to cut traffic congestion
and improve public safety.
(6) Wildfire prevention and resilience projects to
protect lives, homes, and natural resources.
(7) Safe, modernized public schools and educational
facilities for students and educators.
(8) Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
to connect underserved communities and expand
opportunity.
(f) By speeding up these essential projects, the act will
make California more affordable and lower the cost of
housing, energy, electricity, health care, and other
necessities, while also reducing taxpayer costs for
public works projects.
(g) The act will also jump-start projects that create
well-paying jobs and put tens of thousands of
Californians to work, especially in construction, clean
energy, and infrastructure, helping grow California’s
economy when it is needed most.
(h) Importantly, the act maintains state and federal
clean air, clean water, and environmental protection
laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the Safe
Drinking Water Act, the federal Toxic Substances
Control Act, the federal Clean Water Act, the Clean Air
Act, the federal Environmental Quality Improvement
Act, the California Global Warming Solutions Act, the
California Coastal Act, and the federal Resource
Conservation and Recovery Act. This chapter will help
build the projects needed to make California more
affordable, without repealing these laws that keep
families and the environment safe.
(i) We can and must build an affordable California.

PROPOSITION 45
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds sections to the Public
Resources Code; therefore, new provisions proposed to
be added are printed in italic type to indicate that they
are new.
PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section
21010) is added to Division 13 of the Public Resources
Code, to read:
CHAPTER 1.5. BUILDING AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA ACT
Article 1. Title, Findings and Declarations,
and Purpose
21010. Title
This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Building an Affordable California Act.
21011. Findings and Declarations
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare all of the following:
(a) California’s outdated system for approving essential
projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly.
Essential projects like clean water, clean energy,
hospitals, affordable housing, roads, wildfire
prevention, schools, public safety, and other
infrastructure improvements are being delayed or
blocked by unnecessary red tape, bureaucratic delays,
and excessive lawsuits.
(b) These delays substantially increase the cost of
living for all Californians. Research shows that
permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars
to the price of a new home, driving up rents and
mortgages for homeowners and renters. Similar red
tape adds billions of dollars to the cost of building
hospitals, water infrastructure, roads, bridges, clean
energy, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation
projects, costs ultimately passed on to consumers and
taxpayers.
(c) California’s permitting laws were written more than
50 years ago, before today’s modern environmental
laws were in place. That outdated system now works
against the state’s environmental and public health
goals by slowing down or blocking essential projects
that would reduce air pollution, lower greenhouse gas
emissions, safeguard water supplies, protect
communities from wildfire, and preserve wildlife and
the environment.
(d) The act will modernize and streamline state law to
cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays, limit
frivolous lawsuits that block essential projects while
allowing public agencies and essential project
applicants to continue sharing the burden of defending
against those suits, and speed up delivery of projects
Californians rely on every day.
(e) Every year of delay means Californians wait longer
and pay more for the things they need most. The act
applies to the state’s most essential projects, including:
(1) Clean drinking water and secure water supplies for
communities across the state.
(2) Safe, modern hospitals and clinics to ensure access
to affordable health care.
(3) Clean energy and reliable electricity to reduce
energy bills and fight climate change.
(4) Housing of all types in order to make housing more
affordable for families struggling with skyrocketing
rents and mortgages as well as vulnerable senior
populations.
(5) Roads, bridges, and transit to cut traffic congestion
and improve public safety.
(6) Wildfire prevention and resilience projects to
protect lives, homes, and natural resources.
(7) Safe, modernized public schools and educational
facilities for students and educators.
(8) Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
to connect underserved communities and expand
opportunity.
(f) By speeding up these essential projects, the act will
make California more affordable and lower the cost of
housing, energy, electricity, health care, and other
necessities, while also reducing taxpayer costs for
public works projects.
(g) The act will also jump-start projects that create
well-paying jobs and put tens of thousands of
Californians to work, especially in construction, clean
energy, and infrastructure, helping grow California’s
economy when it is needed most.
(h) Importantly, the act maintains state and federal
clean air, clean water, and environmental protection
laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the Safe

CHAPTER 1.5. BUILDING AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA ACT
Article 1. Title, Findings and Declarations,
and Purpose
21010. Title
This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Building an Affordable California Act.
21011. Findings and Declarations
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare all of the following:
(a) California’s outdated system for approving essential
projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly.
Essential projects like clean water, clean energy,
hospitals, affordable housing, roads, wildfire
prevention, schools, public safety, and other
infrastructure improvements are being delayed or
blocked by unnecessary red tape, bureaucratic delays,
and excessive lawsuits.
(b) These delays substantially increase the cost of
living for all Californians. Research shows that
permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars
to the price of a new home, driving up rents and
mortgages for homeowners and renters. Similar red
tape adds billions of dollars to the cost of building
hospitals, water infrastructure, roads, bridges, clean
energy, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation
projects, costs ultimately passed on to consumers and
taxpayers.
(c) California’s permitting laws were written more than
50 years ago, before today’s modern environmental
laws were in place. That outdated system now works
against the state’s environmental and public health
goals by slowing down or blocking essential projects
that would reduce air pollution, lower greenhouse gas
emissions, safeguard water supplies, protect
communities from wildfire, and preserve wildlife and
the environment.
(d) The act will modernize and streamline state law to
cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays, limit
frivolous lawsuits that block essential projects while
allowing public agencies and essential project
applicants to continue sharing the burden of defending
against those suits, and speed up delivery of projects
Californians rely on every day.
(e) Every year of delay means Californians wait longer
and pay more for the things they need most. The act
applies to the state’s most essential projects, including:
(1) Clean drinking water and secure water supplies for
communities across the state.
(2) Safe, modern hospitals and clinics to ensure access
to affordable health care.
(3) Clean energy and reliable electricity to reduce
energy bills and fight climate change.
(4) Housing of all types in order to make housing more
affordable for families struggling with skyrocketing
rents and mortgages as well as vulnerable senior
populations.
(5) Roads, bridges, and transit to cut traffic congestion
and improve public safety.
(6) Wildfire prevention and resilience projects to
protect lives, homes, and natural resources.
(7) Safe, modernized public schools and educational
facilities for students and educators.
(8) Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
to connect underserved communities and expand
opportunity.
(f) By speeding up these essential projects, the act will
make California more affordable and lower the cost of
housing, energy, electricity, health care, and other
necessities, while also reducing taxpayer costs for
public works projects.
(g) The act will also jump-start projects that create
well-paying jobs and put tens of thousands of
Californians to work, especially in construction, clean
energy, and infrastructure, helping grow California’s
economy when it is needed most.
(h) Importantly, the act maintains state and federal
clean air, clean water, and environmental protection
laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the Safe
Drinking Water Act, the federal Toxic Substances
Control Act, the federal Clean Water Act, the Clean Air
Act, the federal Environmental Quality Improvement
Act, the California Global Warming Solutions Act, the
California Coastal Act, and the federal Resource
Conservation and Recovery Act. This chapter will help
build the projects needed to make California more
affordable, without repealing these laws that keep
families and the environment safe.
(i) We can and must build an affordable California.

CHAPTER 1.5. BUILDING AN AFFORDABLE CALIFORNIA ACT
Article 1. Title, Findings and Declarations,
and Purpose
21010. Title
This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Building an Affordable California Act.
21011. Findings and Declarations
The people of the State of California hereby find and
declare all of the following:
(a) California’s outdated system for approving essential
projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly.
Essential projects like clean water, clean energy,
hospitals, affordable housing, roads, wildfire
prevention, schools, public safety, and other
infrastructure improvements are being delayed or
blocked by unnecessary red tape, bureaucratic delays,
and excessive lawsuits.
(b) These delays substantially increase the cost of
living for all Californians. Research shows that
permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars
to the price of a new home, driving up rents and
mortgages for homeowners and renters. Similar red
tape adds billions of dollars to the cost of building
hospitals, water infrastructure, roads, bridges, clean
energy, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation
projects, costs ultimately passed on to consumers and
taxpayers.
(c) California’s permitting laws were written more than
50 years ago, before today’s modern environmental
laws were in place. That outdated system now works
against the state’s environmental and public health
goals by slowing down or blocking essential projects
that would reduce air pollution, lower greenhouse gas
emissions, safeguard water supplies, protect
communities from wildfire, and preserve wildlife and
the environment.
(d) The act will modernize and streamline state law to
cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays, limit
frivolous lawsuits that block essential projects while
allowing public agencies and essential project
applicants to continue sharing the burden of defending
against those suits, and speed up delivery of projects
Californians rely on every day.
(e) Every year of delay means Californians wait longer
and pay more for the things they need most. The act
applies to the state’s most essential projects, including:
(1) Clean drinking water and secure water supplies for
communities across the state.
(2) Safe, modern hospitals and clinics to ensure access
to affordable health care.
(3) Clean energy and reliable electricity to reduce
energy bills and fight climate change.
(4) Housing of all types in order to make housing more
affordable for families struggling with skyrocketing
rents and mortgages as well as vulnerable senior
populations.
(5) Roads, bridges, and transit to cut traffic congestion
and improve public safety.
(6) Wildfire prevention and resilience projects to
protect lives, homes, and natural resources.
(7) Safe, modernized public schools and educational
facilities for students and educators.
(8) Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
to connect underserved communities and expand
opportunity.
(f) By speeding up these essential projects, the act will
make California more affordable and lower the cost of
housing, energy, electricity, health care, and other
necessities, while also reducing taxpayer costs for
public works projects.
(g) The act will also jump-start projects that create
well-paying jobs and put tens of thousands of
Californians to work, especially in construction, clean
energy, and infrastructure, helping grow California’s
economy when it is needed most.
(h) Importantly, the act maintains state and federal
clean air, clean water, and environmental protection
laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the Safe
Drinking Water Act, the federal Toxic Substances
Control Act, the federal Clean Water Act, the Clean Air
Act, the federal Environmental Quality Improvement
Act, the California Global Warming Solutions Act, the
California Coastal Act, and the federal Resource
Conservation and Recovery Act. This chapter will help
build the projects needed to make California more
affordable, without repealing these laws that keep
families and the environment safe.
(i) We can and must build an affordable California.

Let me also note: KQED guide confirms exclusion of Delta conveyance, nuclear, high-speed rail. Editorial support: Southern California News Group (LA Daily News, OC Register), SDUT, Bakersfield Californian, Mercury News/East Bay Times, McClatchy CA (Sac Bee, Fresno, Modesto, Merced, SLO), Santa Cruz Sentinel, WSJ — all Yes. SF Chronicle No; LA Times editorial board no position (but Skelton column No).

Now the decision. Let me weigh carefully.

The case for YES:
1. CEQA has well-documented abuses — NIMBYs blocking infill housing, bike lanes, transit; unions using CEQA for leverage ("greenmail"); endless litigation (UC Berkeley People's Park; Richardson Grove 15 years).
2. California has the worst housing affordability crisis; permitting delays add tens of thousands per home; infrastructure cost overruns.
3. Deadlines (365 days for EIR, 270 days for courts) are reasonable in principle; current deadlines exist but aren't enforced.
4. Broad editorial support (26+ papers), including papers that are usually pro-environment (Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sac Bee).
5. Support from affordable housing groups, children's hospitals, water providers, clean energy (American Clean Power), NAACP, LULAC, Environmental Policy Innovation Center.
6. Projects still must comply with all substantive environmental laws (Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, ESA, Coastal Act); no exemptions from review itself; local governments retain approval/denial authority.
7. Includes labor standards (prevailing wage >85ft housing; skilled-and-trained for public non-housing projects).

The case for NO:
1. Scope creep: bundles genuinely beneficial projects (infill housing, transit, clean energy) with freeway expansions, greenfield sprawl in fire zones, giant warehouses, possibly data centers — with poll-tested exclusions (HSR, Delta tunnel, nuclear) that undercut the policy logic. Since AB 130/SB 131 (2025) already exempted most infill housing, the marginal housing covered is disproportionately sprawl (Tejon Ranch backing is telling — NYT).
2. Structural power shift beyond deadlines: applicant-chosen single "alternative" replaces agency-developed range of alternatives; standards frozen at application; agencies barred from requesting more info; comment caps with late comments excluded from record; courts limited to halting only portions with "specific, adverse impact upon public safety"; interpretive clause giving "fullest possible weight" to approval. Legal experts (Elkind: "sea change"; Sivas: makes CEQA "meaningless"; Elmendorf: unpredictable second-order effects) see it as overreach.
3. Erodes judicial review — the enforcement mechanism of CEQA. If courts can't stop projects and can't consider late evidence, compliance becomes largely voluntary.
4. Tribal consultation narrowed to federally recognized tribes, cutting out dozens of California tribes — and a major funder (San Manuel) is a federally recognized tribe that benefits.
5. Written and funded by interests that profit (utilities Edison/Sempra, CBIA, Chamber, Tejon Ranch, tech); no affordability requirement in text; the "$75,000 savings" is a backer estimate, not guaranteed.
6. Initiative statute locks in 41 pages of highly technical law; hard to fix via Legislature (amendment restrictions), unlike the iterative legislative process already underway (Steinberg's point). If problems emerge, fixes would likely need another ballot measure.
7. Opposition coalition: environmental, public health, nurses, environmental justice, Building Trades, SEIU, CA Dem Party; rural counties rep uncomfortable ("puts power in hands of developers, limits local authority"); YIMBY Action neutral.
8. LAO: upfront costs high tens of millions to >$100M/yr; uncertain long-term effects; possible increased litigation to interpret the law (data centers question will be litigated — ironic).
9. Polling trended against; Newsom declined to endorse despite being a CEQA reformer; several CEQA-reform leaders (Blakespear, Steinberg) oppose.

The crux: Is Prop 45 a surgical fix for genuine CEQA abuse, or an overbroad deregulatory power grab dressed as affordability policy?

The strongest yes argument: deadlines + predictable process + broad newspaper/editorial support + real abuse problem + affordability crisis is the state's top issue.

The strongest no argument: the measure doesn't just impose deadlines — it rewires substantive review (alternatives, standards, record, remedies) for an enormous, poll-tested category set including freeways and sprawl, at a time when the Legislature is actively and iteratively reforming CEQA (AB 130/SB 131 in 2025). Voting yes locks in a 41-page corporate-drafted regime that's hard to amend; voting no preserves momentum for targeted legislative reform. The fact that leading CEQA reformers (Steinberg, Blakespear, Elkind, Elmendorf-cautious, SF Chronicle which has decried CEQA abuse for years) say "right problem, wrong tool" is powerful evidence.

Weighing: I think the better judgment is NO. The measure pairs genuinely good ideas (enforceable deadlines, single completeness list, shot-clock for litigation) with structural changes that shift the balance decisively toward applicants and weaken judicial enforcement — applied not just to the sympathetic projects but to freeways, greenfield sprawl, warehouses, and possibly data centers. When a measure is ballot-box legislation drafted by the Chamber of Commerce with poll-tested exclusions, and even pro-reform voices decline to support it, the prudent vote is No and let the Legislature continue targeted reform (it has shown it will act: SB 131/AB 130, SB 79, etc.).

Counter-consideration: Could one argue the Legislature only acts under pressure, and Prop 45 is the hammer? That's the CalChamber argument. But the Legislature demonstrably acted in 2025 with the biggest CEQA rollback in decades (AB 130/SB 131) — so the "Legislature does nothing" premise is weak in 2026.

Also the "no exemptions" claim is technically true but misleading: the measure rewrites the review itself (alternatives, standards, record, remedies), which is where CEQA's bite lives.

Decision: No.

Structural power shift beyond deadlines: applicant-chosen single "alternative" replaces agency-developed range of alternatives; standards frozen at application; agencies barred from requesting more info; comment caps with late comments excluded from record; courts limited to halting only portions with "specific, adverse impact upon public safety"; interpretive clause giving "fullest possible weight" to approval. Legal experts (Elkind: "sea change"; Sivas: makes CEQA "meaningless"; Elmendorf: unpredictable second-order effects) see it as overreach.
3. Erodes judicial review — the enforcement mechanism of CEQA. If courts can't stop projects and can't consider late evidence, compliance becomes largely voluntary.
4. Tribal consultation narrowed to federally recognized tribes, cutting out dozens of California tribes — and a major funder (San Manuel) is a federally recognized tribe that benefits.
5. Written and funded by interests that profit (utilities Edison/Sempra, CBIA, Chamber, Tejon Ranch, tech); no affordability requirement in text; the "$75,000 savings" is a backer estimate, not guaranteed.
6. Initiative statute locks in 41 pages of highly technical law; hard to fix via Legislature (amendment restrictions), unlike the iterative legislative process already underway (Steinberg's point). If problems emerge, fixes would likely need another ballot measure.
7. Opposition coalition: environmental, public health, nurses, environmental justice, Building Trades, SEIU, CA Dem Party; rural counties rep uncomfortable ("puts power in hands of developers, limits local authority"); YIMBY Action neutral.
8. LAO: upfront costs high tens of millions to >$100M/yr; uncertain long-term effects; possible increased litigation to interpret the law (data centers question will be litigated — ironic).
9. Polling trended against; Newsom declined to endorse despite being a CEQA reformer; several CEQA-reform leaders (Blakespear, Steinberg) oppose.

The crux: Is Prop 45 a surgical fix for genuine CEQA abuse, or an overbroad deregulatory power grab dressed as affordability policy?

The strongest yes argument: deadlines + predictable process + broad newspaper/editorial support + real abuse problem + affordability crisis is the state's top issue.

The strongest no argument: the measure doesn't just impose deadlines — it rewires substantive review (alternatives, standards, record, remedies) for an enormous, poll-tested category set including freeways and sprawl, at a time when the Legislature is actively and iteratively reforming CEQA (AB 130/SB 131 in 2025). Voting yes locks in a 41-page corporate-drafted regime that's hard to amend; voting no preserves momentum for targeted legislative reform. The fact that leading CEQA reformers (Steinberg, Blakespear, Elkind, Elmendorf-cautious, SF Chronicle which has decried CEQA abuse for years) say "right problem, wrong tool" is powerful evidence.

Weighing: I think the better judgment is NO. The measure pairs genuinely good ideas (enforceable deadlines, single completeness list, shot-clock for litigation) with structural changes that shift the balance decisively toward applicants and weaken judicial enforcement — applied not just to the sympathetic projects but to freeways, greenfield sprawl, warehouses, and possibly data centers. When a measure is ballot-box legislation drafted by the Chamber of Commerce with poll-tested exclusions, and even pro-reform voices decline to support it, the prudent vote is No and let the Legislature continue targeted reform (it has shown it will act: SB 131/AB 130, SB 79, etc.).

Counter-consideration: Could one argue the Legislature only acts under pressure, and Prop 45 is the hammer? That's the CalChamber argument. But the Legislature demonstrably acted in 2025 with the biggest CEQA rollback in decades (AB 130/SB 131) — so the "Legislature does nothing" premise is weak in 2026.

Also the "no exemptions" claim is technically true but misleading: the measure rewrites the review itself (alternatives, standards, record, remedies), which is where CEQA's bite lives.

Decision: No.

**No.**

I researched this extensively (the official voter guide, the LAO's impartial analysis, the full initiative text, campaign finance records, polling, expert commentary, and editorial boards). This is the November 3, 2026 measure sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce to amend CEQA.

The short version of my reasoning: CEQA genuinely needs reform — deadlines and curbs on abusive litigation are sensible, and even opponents concede that. But Prop 45 goes far beyond deadlines. It lets applicants dictate a single project "alternative," freezes review standards at application, caps public comment, restricts tribal consultation to federally recognized tribes only, and severely constrains courts (270-day limits, remedies limited to pieces of projects, an interpretive clause tilted toward approval). It applies the same fast track not just to infill housing and clean energy, but to freeway expansions, greenfield sprawl in fire zones, warehouses, and possibly data centers — with poll-tested exclusions (high-speed rail, the Delta tunnel, nuclear) that reveal it's not principled policy.

Tellingly, many leading CEQA *reformers* — the SF Chronicle editorial board (a longtime critic of CEQA abuse), former Senate leader Darrell Steinberg, Sen. Catherine Blakespear, Berkeley and Stanford environmental law scholars, and Gov. Newsom (who stayed neutral) — declined to back it, largely because the Legislature already enacted major CEQA reforms in 2025 (AB 130/SB 131) and is better positioned to keep iterating than a 41-page, corporate-drafted initiative statute that's hard to amend. When the people who spent years fighting CEQA abuse say "right problem, wrong tool," that's decisive for me.

**Vote No.**
